attempts.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
attempts.key_identity: E tau_B(N) >= c R_eff(0,B(N)^c) mu_h(B(N)) with mu_h(B(N)) = N^{psi(beta)+o(1)}.
attempts.method: Exit-time lower bound from effective resistance: compare the exit time from B(N) with the commute time.
attempts.obstruction: Exit-time concentration fails at fixed environment because of trapping at deep wells; the polylog correction is a trapping statement, not a resistance statement.
attempts.result: The commute-time identity gives E^0_h tau_{B(N)^c} >= c R_eff(0, B(N)^c) pi(B(N)) where pi is the reversible measure (volume of the Liouville measure of the box). The volume is N^{psi... } of order N^{2 + 2 beta^2 g ...} in the notation of the notes, i.e. N^{psi(beta)} up to N^{o(1)} by the LQG volume estimates, and R_eff(0, B(N)^c) >= (log N)^{1/2 - o(1)} ... the resistance lower bound available is only polylogarithmic. Hence E tau >= N^{psi(beta)} times a polylog, which is the right exponent, but the problem asks for a bound on tau in probability, not in expectation, with a (log T)^{1/2+delta} correction. Converting expectation to probability needs concentration of the exit time, and the exit time is not concentrated at fixed environment because the walk can be trapped near the maximum: the trapping time at the deepest well has a heavy tail. The exponent statement (T^{1/psi(beta)+o(1)}) follows from the expectation bound plus Markov's inequality in one direction; the precise correction is out of reach with the resistance route.

attempts.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
attempts.key_identity: Wired: |C_max^{(w)}| = n^{d-1}(1 + sum_r P(one-arm to distance r)) = Theta(n^{d-1}) by the extrinsic one-arm exponent 2; the limit constant requires C0066.
attempts.method: Heuristic derivation of the three scalings and identification of the rigorous gaps.
attempts.obstruction: Boundary-sensitive cluster-size tails for bulk/zero conditions; sharp one-arm constant for the wired constant.
attempts.result: Free/zero boundary: the largest cluster among about n^d / n^4 ... the box contains clusters whose sizes have tail P(|C| >= k) ~ k^{-1/2} in mean field, cut off at the box scale where the cluster diameter ~ k^{1/4} reaches n, i.e. k ~ n^4; the number of clusters of size about n^4 in the box is n^d P(|C(0)| ~ n^4)/n^4 ~ n^{d-6} which is large for d > 6, and the maximum of n^{d-6} clusters with tail k^{-1/2} cut off at n^4 gives the log n factor through the extreme-value count, hence n^4 log n. Rigorous status: the upper bound n^4 log n follows from the cluster-size tail and a union bound; the matching lower bound needs the tail near the cutoff to be exactly of the mean-field form k^{-1/2} up to constants for k up to c n^4 inside a box with boundary, which is a boundary-condition-sensitive statement (the two-point function near the boundary decays faster). Wired boundary: the boundary is one cluster of size n^{d-1} plus the vertices connected to it, the latter of order n^{d-1} times the expected number of vertices connected to the boundary per boundary vertex (~ sum over distance r of r^{d-1} r^{-(d-2)} ... the two-point function summed over a half-space gives order n^2, so the wired giant should be n^{d-1} times a constant only if the connection density to the boundary is summable, which it is in d > 6 only after the one-arm exponent: P(0 <-> boundary at distance r) ~ r^{-2}, and the sum over the box of r^{-2} is n^{d-2}, dominated by the boundary itself... so the constant a_w exists iff the total number of vertices connected to the boundary from distance >= 1 is O(n^{d-1}), which follows from the extrinsic one-arm exponent 2 (Kozma-Nachmias) by summing r^{-2} over the layers r <= n: sum_r n^{d-1} r^{-2} = O(n^{d-1}). So the wired scaling n^{d-1} up to constants is rigorous from the known one-arm exponent; the existence of the limit constant a_w needs the sharp one-arm asymptotics (C0066). Bulk and zero cases remain open at the level of the lower bound.

attempts.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
attempts.method: Decoupling plus the linear Littlewood-Offord bound, to see where the logarithm enters.
attempts.obstruction: The known inverse Littlewood-Offord theorems carry logarithmic losses.
attempts.result: Decoupling Q by splitting the index set into two halves I, J gives P(Q = z) <= P(|sum_{i in I, j in J} c_ij xi_i xi'_j - ...| small)^{1/2}-type bounds where, conditionally on the J-variables, the bilinear form is a linear form in the I-variables with coefficients a_i = sum_j c_ij xi_j; the linear Littlewood-Offord (Erdos) bound gives P <= C/sqrt(number of nonzero a_i), and the a_i are nonzero with high probability except on an event where many coefficient sums vanish, whose probability is itself controlled by a Littlewood-Offord bound on the rows; the loss comes from the union over rows and the conditioning, which is where the n^{o(1)} or logarithmic factors enter in the known proofs. The extremal example (xi_1 + ... + xi_n)^2 shows n^{-1/2} is the right order because the square of a sum concentrates on O(sqrt n) values. To remove the logarithm one needs a rank-type inverse theorem: if P(Q = z) >= n^{-1/2} C then the coefficient matrix is close to rank one with arithmetic structure, and the inverse theorems available (Nguyen-Vu) give such structure only at the cost of a logarithmic loss in the threshold. No improvement obtained; the reduction to a lossless inverse theorem is recorded.

attempts.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
attempts.key_identity: LPS: free MSF is a tree iff no percolation at criticality (plus uniqueness above); continuum high-d lace expansion gives no percolation at criticality; hence a tree in high d, conditionally.
attempts.method: Relate connectivity of the MSF to critical percolation of the Boolean/Gilbert model and to the number of infinite clusters at criticality.
attempts.obstruction: Transfer of the LPS criterion to Poisson processes and the exact statement of the high-d continuum result not verified from fetched sources.
attempts.result: By the Lyons-Peres-Schramm correspondence, the (free) MSF of an invariant point process is a single tree iff, in the associated continuum percolation (Gilbert graph with radius r), there is a.s. no infinite cluster at the critical radius r_c... more precisely the MSF is connected iff for every r there are no two infinite clusters of the r-graph that... their criterion (for Z^d bond percolation) is: the free MSF has one tree iff theta(p_c) = 0 and there is a unique infinite cluster for all p > p_c, under the additional condition that critical percolation has no infinite cluster in the 'invaded' sense; for Z^d they show the free MSF is a tree if theta(p_c) = 0 and every p > p_c has a unique infinite cluster (which holds), so on Z^d the MSF is a single tree iff theta(p_c) = 0. Transferring to the Poisson Gilbert model in R^d: uniqueness above criticality holds (Meester-Roy), and absence of percolation at r_c is known in d = 2 (Alexander's route) and is the continuum analogue of C0023 for d >= 3, known in high dimensions? The continuum Gilbert model in high d does not have a lace-expansion proof of theta(r_c) = 0 as far as I know (the Poisson-Boolean model's mean-field behaviour in high d is established by Heydenreich-van der Hofstad-Last-Matzke 2019 through a lace expansion for the random connection model, which gives theta(r_c) = 0 in high dimensions). So: for d large, theta(r_c) = 0 holds by the random-connection-model lace expansion, and then the LPS criterion gives that the MSF IS a tree, CONTRADICTING the source's suspicion that it is not a tree in high dimension, unless the LPS criterion has an extra hypothesis failing in the continuum. Checking: LPS prove for Z^d that theta(p_c) = 0 implies the free MSF is a tree using that the free MSF equals the union over p of the invasion structures and that the number of trees equals the number of 'p_c-critical infinite clusters'; their argument uses only invariance and the percolation properties, so it should transfer to the Poisson Gilbert model. Hence, conditional on (i) the transfer of the LPS criterion and (ii) theta(r_c) = 0 for the Gilbert model in high d (HvdHLM 2019 for the random connection model), the MSF of the Poisson process IS a single tree in high dimensions, resolving the source's question in the direction opposite to its suspicion. I could not verify (i) and (ii) against fetched texts; recorded as a conditional resolution with the opposite sign of the source's guess, which itself deserves independent review.

attempts.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
attempts.key_identity: Somewhere along Z, windows of n consecutive gaps have arbitrarily small total, so no monotone map has bounded multiplicative distortion; a quasi-isometry must be a non-monotone matching.
attempts.method: Construct an explicit bijection with bounded distortion using the law of the iterated logarithm.
attempts.obstruction: Existence of a bounded-distortion non-monotone matching between two independent Poisson processes is unresolved.
attempts.result: Order both processes as ...< x_{-1} < x_0 < x_1 < ... and ...< y_{-1} < y_0 < y_1 < ... and map x_i -> y_i. Distortion: |y_i - y_j| versus |x_i - x_j| for i < j are both sums of j - i i.i.d. exponentials, so their ratio is close to 1 for large j - i by the law of large numbers, but a quasi-isometry needs a UNIFORM bound C such that |x_i - x_j|/C - c <= |y_i - y_j| <= C|x_i - x_j| + c for ALL pairs; for nearby pairs (j - i small) the ratio of two independent Gamma(k) variables is unbounded over infinitely many pairs (there are a.s. pairs with x-gap tiny and y-gap of order 1), so the index map fails. A quasi-isometry may send x_i to y_{sigma(i)} for a non-monotone sigma, but any quasi-isometry of R-like spaces is at bounded distance from a monotone one, and the additive constant c absorbs bounded gaps: with c >= 1 the small-gap problem disappears for gaps below 1, and the issue becomes long runs of small gaps in one process against long runs of large gaps in the other, i.e. whether for every n the partial sums S_n(x) and S_n(y) of the gaps satisfy S_n(y) <= C S_n(x) + c uniformly in n and in the starting index. By the LIL both partial sums are n + O(sqrt(n log log n)) along a fixed start, but uniformly over all starting indices the fluctuations of a window of length n are of order sqrt(n log(N/n))... over a range of N windows, which stays o(n), so the ratio S_n(y)/S_n(x) is uniformly close to 1 for n large, and for n small the additive constant absorbs the difference. This gives a bounded-distortion index map, i.e. the answer appears to be YES with the identity index map after choosing c large: for every i < j, |y_i - y_j| <= C|x_i - x_j| + c with C = 2 and c depending on the realisation (a.s. finite), because the maximal deviation of window sums of length n over all windows in a range of length N is O(sqrt(n log N)) and the constraint fails only if a window of length n has x-sum < n/2 and y-sum > 2n... which for n >= n_0 has probability exp(-cn) per window, summable over windows of length n at positions up to e^{cn/2}, hence by Borel-Cantelli only finitely many bad windows in total? The windows are infinitely many for each n (positions in Z), so the count is not summable: for fixed n there are infinitely many windows and each is bad with positive probability, so bad windows of each length occur a.s. somewhere. Therefore the uniform constant must absorb the worst window of each length n: the worst x-sum over all windows of length n is 0 in the limit (arbitrarily small sums occur somewhere), which breaks any multiplicative constant. So the naive index map FAILS, and a quasi-isometry needs to map indices non-monotonically to compensate density fluctuations, which for one-dimensional spaces with ergodic gap sequences is a matching problem; the question is genuinely open at this level of analysis. Recorded: index map fails by unbounded density fluctuations; the question is a stationary matching question.

attempts.method: Zero speed on every bounded-degree subexponential-growth subgraph
attempts.obstruction: It settles the zero-speed equivalence for subexponential-growth Cayley graphs and their clusters only. Exponential-growth cases need different information.
attempts.result: Let H be a connected subgraph of a bounded-degree graph G with |B_G(x,n)|=exp(o(n)). The Carne-Varopoulos bound gives P_x(X_n=y)<=2 sqrt(deg_H(y)/deg_H(x)) exp(-d_H(x,y)^2/(2n)). Summing over reachable vertices yields P(d_H(x,X_n)>=epsilon n)<=C exp(o(n)-epsilon^2 n/2), which is summable. Thus the intrinsic speed on H is zero almost surely.

Set a=log10 and K_R(s)=1/[2*(cosh(s)-cosR)], F_R(u)=(K_R(u-a)+K_R(u+a))/2. Choose the unique R in[pi/2,pi) such that R/sinR=t/10. Lemma4.1 then asks whether F_R(u)=1/10 has at most two roots.
